text.text:
#### The Evolution of Mathematics

Mathematical knowledge developed independently in different places, and it was only unified over time by our species — and we have already studied these ideas in earlier classes.

In this class, we will take a tour that highlights maps and the approximate periods when each numerical system appeared, according to our current understanding. The map below shows the journey of our species across the world.

text.text:
#### In Africa: Counting with Bones

The first counting system we know of arose in Africa about 37,000 years ago. It was inspired by our hands and was recorded with marks made on bones. Scholars such as Francisco A. González Redondo study these marks to understand when counting began.
*Figure: Africa on the world map.*

source_menu.text: González Redondo, Francisco A., et al.

text.text:
#### In Africa: Practicing with Bones

Each mark carved on the bone represents one count. Use the buttons to add or remove marks until the bone shows the proposed number.

#### In America: The Quipus

The second counting system we learn about did not arise near the first one. The earliest evidence dates from about 5,000 years ago. Although some researchers still doubt how old the quipus are, here we follow the researchers who argue that they were already present in Caral, Peru, unless new research proves otherwise.

text.imgdesc: *Figure: South America on the world map.*

text.text: *Figure: South America on the world map.*

#### In America: Practice with Quipu

The quipu is read on the vertical cords that hang from the main horizontal cord, and each knot represents a count. Add knots until the cord shows the proposed number.

Represent the proposed number with the quipu.

#### In America: The Mesoamerican Numbers

Recent research suggests that a numerical system began to develop in Mesoamerica around <htdate0>. This may extend our earlier understanding, which placed their use around 300 BCE.

text.imgdesc: *Figure: Mesoamerica on the map of North America.*

text.text: *Figure: Mesoamerica on the map of North America.*

#### In America: Practicing with Mesoamerican Numbers

In the Mesoamerican system, a dot is worth 1 and a bar is worth 5. Use the buttons to build the proposed number with dots and bars.

#### In Europe: The Calculi

We cannot be sure that Caral, Peru, was the first place to make quipus, because quipus are not easy to preserve over time. The same issue happens with the abacus.

For this reason, we start our tour with the *calculi*, whose use the papers we consulted date to around <htdate0>.
*Figure: Europe on the world map.*

#### In Europe: Practice with Calculi

On the calculi, each column has a different place value. Markers below the bar are worth 1 and markers above the bar are worth 5. Move the markers toward the bar to represent the proposed number.

#### In Asia (India): The Hindu-Arabic Numerals

We cannot be sure when the Hindu-Arabic numerals first arose: writing systems reached India only about 2,300 years ago, though numbers may have existed before that.

For this reason, we include Hindu numerals here: they appear in the Ashoka inscriptions dated to <htdate0> and <htdate1>.
*Figure: Asia on the world map.*

#### In Asia: Practicing Hindu-Arabic

In a sequence, each number follows the one before it by a fixed step. Look at the sequence and choose the number that is missing.

#### In Asia (China): The Suanpan

Around <htdate0>, we have the first information about the *suanpan* (算盤), the Chinese abacus. This abacus differs from the *calculi* because it has a different number of beads.
*Figure: Asia on the world map.*

#### In Asia (China): Practicing Suanpan

Write the proposed number on the suanpan by moving the beads.

#### In America: The Yupana

Returning to America (Abya Yala), we know that the Incas — during the 15th and 16th centuries according to the Gregorian calendar — created a tool to do mathematics. More than that, we have evidence that the *yupana* was used together with the *quipus*.

In this app, we explore the Yupana Inka Tawa Pukllay method, developed by Dhavit Prem, to learn how to use this ancient tool.
*Figure: South America (Tawantinsuyu) on the map.*

#### In America: Practicing with Yupana

On the yupana, each row holds one digit, and the seeds are placed in the cells. Use the buttons to represent the proposed number on the row.

#### In Asia (Japan): The Soroban

During the 16th century, according to the Gregorian calendar, the *suanpan* (算盤) reached Japan, where it became known as the *soroban* (算盤). This soroban is the closest approximation to the Roman *calculi* we saw earlier in this class.
*Figure: Asia on the world map.*

#### In Asia (Japan): Practicing Soroban

Write the proposed number on the soroban by moving the beads.

#### In Russia: The Schyoty

Around <htdate0>, in Russia, another tool used to represent numbers was developed. Although some people call it an abacus, we cannot evaluate possible connections between it and the earlier abacuses we studied here.
*Figure: Asia on the world map.*

#### In Russia: Practicing Schyoty

Write the proposed number on the schyoty by moving the beads.

#### Conclusion

In this class, we reviewed different numerical systems and observed that the time when they were created does not follow the path of human occupation of the world.

As a result, we can reach some conclusions:
- We are all human, and knowledge did not arise in one place and then spread around the world.
- The basis of mathematics was always everywhere.
- We can reach the same conclusions by representing numbers in different ways.

In the next classes, we will learn how to work with these numbers.
